claims.text: The proposed computational approach combines cluster expansion with effective medium theory.
The proposed approach can predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivities of HfNbTaTiZr separately.
The proposed approach will reduce prediction error by more than 25% relative to prior models.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr is a bulk crystal with controlled local chemical disorder and up to 1 wt.% oxygen.
The combined framework captures local fluctuations in atomic mass, force constants, and oxygen-induced disorder.
Below 200 K, the individual lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are experimentally measurable.
Experimental total thermal-conductivity data for HfNbTaTiZr are available from 300 to 1200 K.
Cluster-expansion coefficients can quantify local chemical disorder and lattice fluctuations associated with mass, force-constant, and impurity variations.
Cluster expansion accurately represents each atom's local environment.
Feeding cluster-expansion parameters into effective medium theory decouples lattice and electronic heat transport.
Representing local environments avoids oversimplifications caused by an average Debye temperature and idealized-lattice assumptions.
The model's separated lattice and electronic conductivity predictions will match experimental low-temperature trends.
The model's combined thermal conductivity will match experimental trends between 300 and 1200 K.
Existing DFT-derived elastic-property and analytical approaches require an assumed Debye temperature.
Existing baseline approaches do not decouple lattice and electronic conduction pathways and assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The model is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr samples with defect and impurity profiles similar to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model's validated temperature domains are below 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K.
Predictive performance may diminish when impurity concentrations or microstructural-defect populations differ substantially from the stated constraints.
The magnitude of the error reduction is sensitive to cluster-expansion fit accuracy and impurity representation.
Failure to achieve at least a 25% error reduction relative to baseline models would falsify the hypothesis.
